paras: The lynching of Frank Varner was the reported hanging and shooting of a Black man taken from the jail at Fort Worth, Texas, in March 1881, a few hours after he was jailed on a charge of assaulting a young woman. The story reached newspapers across the country through a single St. Louis Republican special, and only one copy of it, in the Cheyenne Daily Leader, reported the lynching; every other copy ended with the prediction that Varner "will probably be lynched."

According to the special, dated March 17, Varner, described as "a negro," was accused of choking, beating and gagging Laura Edison, "a handsome and quite accomplished young lady" living two miles from Fort Worth, and of raping her. Some copies gave his name as Frank Warner, Frank Varna or Frank Vairer, and hers as Luana Edison.

After the alleged assault Varner fled, but "friends of the lady" pursued him, captured him and lodged him in jail. The Cheyenne Daily Leader's copy added that "a few hours latter a party of men surrounded the jail," took Varner out, led him to a tree, put a rope around his neck, strung him up, and filled his body with bullets. Neither the time of day, the location of the tree, the size of the party nor the presence of any officers is stated.
No report of an inquest, of arrests of the lynching party or of any official response appears in the coverage, and no Texas paper's account was found.

The special ran on March 18 in the Daily Globe, the Memphis Daily Appeal, the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer, the Chicago Daily Tribune and the Cheyenne Daily Leader, with shorter summaries in the Public Ledger and the Sacramento Daily Record-Union. Western papers such as the Carson City Morning Appeal and the Eureka Daily Sentinel carried it on March 19 under a Fort Worth, March 18 dateline, and weeklies in Montana, Minnesota and elsewhere reprinted it in crime digests through March 24, one of them misprinting the city as "Fort North."

Headlines treated a lynching as fitting or expected: the Globe headed the item "A Customer for Judge Lynch," the Tribune "A Case for Judge Lynch," the Memphis paper "His Chances Are Good," and the Wheeling paper "He Ought to Re[Be]." The Cheyenne paper, the only one to report the hanging, titled it "One Villain Less," and the Eureka paper's headline read "A Young Lady Brutally Outraged by a Negro." None of the papers questioned the accusation, named a witness, or reported Varner's own account.

Whether Varner was killed rests on the Cheyenne copy alone, which carries the same St. Louis dateline and opening text as the others but adds the lynching. The other copies, including weekly digests printed nearly a week later, still described him as lodged in jail and likely to be lynched, and no follow-up confirming or denying his death was found.

bases: One copy of the Fort Worth special reports that a party of men took Varner from jail, hanged him from a tree and shot him (A5); every other copy ends with him jailed and 'will probably be lynched' (A1, A2, A4).

All copies descend from one St. Louis Republican Fort Worth special (A1, A4, A5); the lynching itself appears only in the Cheyenne Daily Leader's copy (A5) and no local, follow-up or independent report was found.
